title: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array (check `num % 2 == 0`).
shortTitle: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array

s1_definition.profdef: Separating even and odd numbers is a linear pass where you test each integer with the modulo operator. If `num % 2 == 0` the number is even, otherwise it is odd, and you route it into the matching collection. It is O(n) time, and O(n) space to hold the two result lists.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India assigns each account a numeric branch-batch id. For a maintenance window they process even-numbered batches on one server and odd-numbered batches on another to split the load. A clerk reads each batch id and drops it into the "even" tray or the "odd" tray.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each number, if dividing by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise odd — route it accordingly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Separating even and odd numbers is a linear pass where you test each integer with the modulo operator. If `num % 2 == 0` the number is even, otherwise it is odd, and you route it into the matching collection. It is O(n) time, and O(n) space to hold the two result lists.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India assigns each account a numeric branch-batch id. For a maintenance window they process even-numbered batches on one server and odd-numbered batches on another to split the load. A clerk reads each batch id and drops it into the "even" tray or the "odd" tray.

**One line to remember:** For each number, if dividing by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise odd — route it accordingly.

sections.s2_technical:
The modulo operator `%` gives the remainder of integer division. `num % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for positive odd numbers. So the test `num % 2 == 0` cleanly classifies each value. You loop once over the array, apply the test, and add each number to either the evens list or the odds list.

A nuance is negative numbers: in Java, `-3 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`, because the result takes the sign of the dividend. So the robust odd test is `num % 2 != 0` rather than `num % 2 == 1`, which would wrongly classify negative odds. In our banking batch ids the numbers are positive, but writing `!= 0` is the safe habit.

Time is O(n) for the single pass. Space is O(n) to store the two lists, which together hold all n elements. If you only needed to print and not store, you could print inside the loop and use O(1) extra space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a nightly batch and wants to split work across two servers by batch id: even ids go to server A, odd ids to server B. The system must separate a list of batch ids into evens and odds. This is exactly how the even-odd split works — test each with modulo and route it.

Problem 2 — Some cancelled batches carry negative sentinel ids, and we must still classify them correctly. This is exactly why we test odd as remainder not equal to zero rather than remainder equal to one, because in Java a negative odd number gives a remainder of minus one.

The code has a `BatchSplitter` class with a `split` method returning a holder of two lists. The demo splits a list of batch ids and logs both lists.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: batch ids `[101, 202, 303, 404, -5, 600]`.

Step 1 — `101 % 2` is 1, so it is odd. Odds: `[101]`.

Step 2 — `202 % 2` is 0, so it is even. Evens: `[202]`.

Step 3 — `303 % 2` is 1, so it is odd. Odds: `[101, 303]`.

Step 4 — `404 % 2` is 0, so it is even. Evens: `[202, 404]`.

Step 5 — `-5 % 2` is -1, which is not zero, so it is odd. The `!= 0` logic classifies it correctly. Odds: `[101, 303, -5]`.

Step 6 — `600 % 2` is 0, so it is even. Evens: `[202, 404, 600]`.

Step 7 — Return both lists and log them.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Even batches (server A): [202, 404, 600]
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Odd batches (server B):  [101, 303, -5]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: [101, 202, 303, 404, -5, 600]
    │
    ▼
  BatchSplitter.split()
    │ 101 %2=1 ──→ odds
    │ 202 %2=0 ──→ evens
    │ 303 %2=1 ──→ odds
    │ 404 %2=0 ──→ evens
    │ -5  %2=-1≠0 ──→ odds   (negative handled by !=0)
    │ 600 %2=0 ──→ evens
    ▼
  SplitResult{ evens=[202,404,600], odds=[101,303,-5] }
    │
    ▼
  Log evens → server A, odds → server B
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Separating even and odd numbers is a single linear pass where I test each integer with the modulo operator. If a number divided by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise it is odd, and I route it into the appropriate collection. The pass is linear time, and I use linear space to hold the two result lists.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to split nightly batch work across two servers. Each batch carries a numeric id, and I send even-numbered batches to one server and odd-numbered batches to another to balance the load.

The nuance I always mention is negative numbers. In Java the modulo operator keeps the sign of the dividend, so a negative odd number like minus five gives a remainder of minus one, not plus one. If I tested for odd by checking whether the remainder equals one, I would wrongly classify every negative odd number. So the robust test is to check whether the remainder is not equal to zero, which correctly identifies odd numbers regardless of sign. In our batch ids a cancelled batch can carry a negative sentinel id, so handling that correctly matters in production.
